\section{Introduction}
\label{sec:introduction}

When multilingual large language models (LLMs) encounter conflicting information across languages, the language of presentation can determine which answer the model produces.
\citet{zhao2026when} showed that linguistic affinity dominates conflict resolution in entity-centric factual conflicts, with models preferring answers from linguistically closer sources.
Yet the internal mechanism behind this behavior remains opaque: how does the model encode the conflict signal?
Can it be detected from internal representations?
And if detectable, does the detected signal causally influence the model's resolution strategy?
These questions sit at the intersection of mechanistic interpretability and multilingual NLP, and answering them requires moving beyond behavioral observations to probe model internals directly.

Existing work on probing knowledge conflict signals has been limited to monolingual settings.
\citet{zhao2024analysing} showed that residual stream representations carry linearly detectable conflict signals in English, and \citet{boer2026probing} performed knowledge attribution probing to localize factual associations within model parameters.
Extending these approaches cross-lingually introduces additional challenges.
Translation quality may confound probe transfer: a poor translation could alter conflict detection for reasons unrelated to the conflict signal itself.
Token overlap between languages, even when minimal, could provide a shortcut for cross-lingual probes.
Observed asymmetries in transfer accuracy may reflect general cross-lingual properties rather than conflict-specific phenomena, and disentangling these sources requires careful baseline comparisons.
Beyond detectability, a fundamental limitation of probing is that it establishes correlation, not causation \citep{hewitt2019designing}.
\citet{basu2026interpretability} demonstrated that even near-perfect probe accuracy does not guarantee that the detected direction can steer model behavior.

We address these questions through a pipeline (Figure~\ref{fig:pipeline}) that combines residual stream probing with representation steering across two models of distinct architectures: Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct and Qwen3-8B.
Probes achieve 77.1\% and 75.3\% balanced accuracy on English within-language conflict detection, respectively, and all cross-lingual transfer directions exceed chance (binomial $p < 0.001$).
Cross-lingual transfer exhibits a directional asymmetry: probes trained on Chinese transfer to English approximately 7 percentage points (pp) more accurately than the reverse in both models.
This asymmetry, however, is not conflict-specific.
XNLI entailment-versus-contradiction probes \citep{conneau2018xnli} show the same directional pattern at comparable magnitude (+6.0 and +6.7 pp), with substantially overlapping confidence intervals.
The conflict asymmetry thus inherits from a general property of English-dominant models, where Chinese representations project more readily onto English representational space than the reverse.
Our causal analysis reveals a dissociation between detection and decision: the probe signal peaks at late layers (L28, 88\% depth), but representation steering succeeds only at a mid-layer (L13, 41\% depth; Fisher $p = 0.002$), with all late-layer interventions producing no significant behavioral change.
To ensure these findings are robust, we apply a confound exclusion pipeline that includes COMET-based translation quality stratification, token overlap analysis, and non-conflict baseline comparison.

These results carry two methodological implications.
The layer dissociation between probing peak and causal influence demonstrates that the layer with highest probe accuracy is not necessarily where the model resolves the conflict.
This challenges the common practice of intervening at the probing peak layer, consistent with the warning from \citet{basu2026interpretability} that detectability and causal relevance can diverge.
The directional asymmetry in cross-lingual transfer reflects a structural property of English-dominant multilingual models, not a conflict-specific phenomenon.
Any cross-lingual probing study must account for this baseline asymmetry to correctly interpret transfer differences.

Our contributions are as follows:
\begin{itemize}
    \item \textbf{Cross-lingual conflict detectability and asymmetry characterization.} We provide the first evidence that knowledge conflict signals are linearly detectable across languages in residual stream representations. The transfer asymmetry (ZH$\to$EN $>$ EN$\to$ZH by ${\sim}$7 pp) matches the XNLI non-conflict baseline in both magnitude and direction, establishing that it reflects the model's general cross-lingual structure rather than conflict-specific encoding.
    \item \textbf{Detection-decision layer dissociation.} Representation steering at the mid-layer (L13, 41\% depth) causally shifts conflict resolution (Fisher $p = 0.002$), while steering at the late-layer probing peak (L28, 88\% depth) produces no significant effect. This dissociation shows that linear detectability does not imply causal relevance, and that conflict resolution occurs upstream of where the outcome becomes linearly readable.
    \item \textbf{Confound exclusion pipeline for cross-lingual probing.} We design and validate a systematic pipeline of COMET translation quality ablation, token overlap analysis, and non-conflict task baseline comparison that excludes common confounds in cross-lingual probing studies.
\end{itemize}

\section{Related Work}
\label{sec:related_work}

\paragraph{Knowledge conflict detection.}
Research on how LLMs handle conflicting knowledge has developed along two axes: behavioral characterization and internal signal analysis.
\citet{xie2024adaptive} introduced ConflictQA and showed that models exhibit context-dependent strategies when parametric and contextual knowledge disagree, ranging from faithful context-following to stubborn reliance on memorized answers.
\citet{xu2024knowledge} provided a systematic taxonomy of conflict types (intra-memory, context-memory, and inter-context) that has since guided experimental design in this area.
More recent work has moved beyond behavioral observation to probe model internals.
\citet{zhao2024analysing} demonstrated that residual stream representations carry linearly separable conflict signals in English, while \citet{boer2026probing} used probing classifiers to localize factual associations within model parameters.
\citet{pham2026where} investigated the mechanistic pathways through which intra-memory conflicts are processed, and \citet{li2025taming} proposed methods to mitigate conflict-induced errors.
These studies, however, operate exclusively in monolingual English settings.
Extending conflict probing to cross-lingual scenarios introduces confounds that require explicit control: translation quality can degrade the conflict signal, token overlap between languages can provide spurious shortcuts, and general cross-lingual transfer properties can be mistaken for conflict-specific phenomena.
We build on the residual stream probing approach of \citet{zhao2024analysing} and extend it to cross-lingual settings with a confound exclusion pipeline that addresses each of these concerns.

\paragraph{Cross-lingual representations in multilingual models.}
A consistent finding across multilingual model analyses is that intermediate layers develop language-independent representations.
\citet{wu2020emerging} showed that cross-lingual structure emerges in pretrained models without explicit alignment objectives, and \citet{muller2021first} found that multilingual BERT first aligns representations across languages in middle layers before making task predictions.
For decoder-only LLMs, \citet{wendler2024llamas} provided evidence that Llama models process non-English inputs through an English-centric latent space, with internal representations converging toward English regardless of the input language.
\citet{kargaran2024mexa} quantified this English-centric bias and showed that cross-lingual alignment quality varies substantially across language pairs and model layers.
This body of work predicts two patterns that we observe empirically.
First, the success of mid-layer steering (L13, 41\% depth) aligns with the finding that language-independent encoding peaks at intermediate layers.
Second, the ZH$\to$EN transfer advantage in our probing experiments is consistent with the English-centric structure documented by \citet{wendler2024llamas} and \citet{kargaran2024mexa}: Chinese representations map more readily onto the English space than the reverse.
Several studies have documented behavioral consequences of this representational structure.
\citet{wang2025lost} found systematic cross-lingual factual inconsistencies in transformer language models, \citet{zhao2026when} constructed the CLEAR benchmark showing that conflict resolution patterns differ across languages, and \citet{ifergan2024beneath} and \citet{xing2024evaluating} evaluated the consistency of cross-lingual knowledge sharing.
Our work complements these behavioral studies by providing a mechanistic account of why such asymmetries arise.

\paragraph{Representation steering and causal intervention.}
Probing establishes correlation between representations and task-relevant information, but causal influence requires intervention.
\citet{li2023iti} introduced Inference-Time Intervention, which adds learned bias vectors at specific attention heads to steer model outputs toward truthfulness.
\citet{zou2023representation} generalized this idea through Representation Engineering, which extracts and manipulates concept-level directions in activation space.
In the knowledge conflict domain, \citet{zhao2025steering} applied SAE-based steering (SpARE) to shift conflict resolution behavior in monolingual settings.
These successes, however, are not universal.
\citet{basu2026interpretability} showed that near-perfect probe accuracy on clinical NLP tasks failed to translate into effective steering, which raises the question of when detectability implies actionability.
\citet{feng2026finegrained} proposed fine-grained activation steering to improve intervention precision by targeting specific layers and positions.
Our results contribute to this discussion by identifying layer selection as a critical variable: mid-layer intervention succeeds where late-layer intervention fails, even though the late layer achieves higher probe accuracy.
This dissociation between the probing peak and the causal locus suggests that conflict resolution occurs upstream of where the outcome becomes linearly readable.

1	\section{Experiments}
2	\label{sec:experiments}
3	
4	\subsection{Experimental Setup}
5	\label{sec:setup}
6	
7	\paragraph{Models.}
8	We probe two instruction-tuned models with comparable parameter counts but distinct architectures: Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct (32 layers, hidden dimension 4096) \citep{grattafiori2024llama} and Qwen3-8B (36 layers, hidden dimension 4096) \citep{yang2024qwen25}.
9	
10	\paragraph{Dataset.}
11	We use ConflictQA \citep{xie2024adaptive}, a benchmark of context-parametric knowledge conflicts where a provided context contradicts the model's parametric knowledge.
12	After verifying that each model can correctly answer the parametric-knowledge question without context, we retain 1{,}368 samples for Llama (1{,}096 train / 272 test) and 966 samples for Qwen (773 train / 193 test), split 80/20 with stratification.
13	
14	\paragraph{Translation.}
15	We translate all English contexts and questions into Chinese using a Qwen3-8B translation pipeline (EN$\to$ZH), with quality validated by COMET \citep{rei2020comet} back-translation scores.
16	
17	\paragraph{Probing.}
18	For each layer $l$, we train a logistic regression probe on the last-token residual stream representation $\mathbf{h}_l$, with binary labels indicating whether the model chose the contextual or parametric answer.
19	We report balanced accuracy to account for class imbalance.
20	All confidence intervals (CIs) are computed via bootstrap resampling with paired differences for asymmetry estimation.
21	
22	\paragraph{Non-conflict baseline.}
23	To test whether cross-lingual transfer patterns are specific to knowledge conflicts, we run the same probing pipeline on XNLI \citep{conneau2018xnli}, classifying entailment versus contradiction.
24	
25	\subsection{Within-Language Conflict Detection}
26	\label{sec:within_lang}
27	
28	Table~\ref{tab:main_results} reports balanced accuracy for all probe transfer directions.
29	Both models encode linearly detectable conflict signals in their residual streams.
30	Llama achieves 77.1\% on EN$\to$EN (peak at layer 28, 88\% depth) and 71.2\% on ZH$\to$ZH.
31	Qwen reaches 75.3\% on EN$\to$EN (peak at layer 22, 61\% depth) and 71.6\% on ZH$\to$ZH.
32	All within-language accuracies are significantly above chance (binomial $p < 0.001$).
33	Figure~\ref{fig:layer_probe} shows the layer-wise probe accuracy curves for both models.
34	These results confirm that knowledge conflict signals are linearly separable in the residual stream across both architectures and both languages.
35	
36	\subsection{Cross-Lingual Transfer and Asymmetry}
37	\label{sec:cross_lingual}
38	
39	All four cross-lingual transfer directions achieve balanced accuracy above chance (binomial $p < 0.001$; Table~\ref{tab:main_results}), confirming that conflict representations partially overlap across languages.
40	Both models show a consistent directional trend: probes trained on Chinese representations transfer to English (ZH$\to$EN) more accurately than the reverse direction (EN$\to$ZH).
41	For Llama, $\Delta_{\text{asym}} = +7.2$ percentage points (pp) with a 95\% bootstrap CI of [1.1, 13.6]; for Qwen, $\Delta_{\text{asym}} = +7.2$ pp with CI [$-$0.6, 13.7].

72	If the ZH$\to$EN transfer advantage were specific to knowledge conflicts, it should be absent or substantially reduced in a non-conflict semantic task.
73	We test this prediction using XNLI entailment-versus-contradiction probes.
74	Both models achieve high within-language accuracy on XNLI (Llama 94.0\% EN, 87.5\% ZH; Qwen 96.6\% EN, 89.5\% ZH), confirming that the probing pipeline captures semantic distinctions beyond knowledge conflicts.

114	\label{sec:steering}
115	
116	The probing results establish that conflict signals are detectable, but detection does not imply causal relevance.
117	We test whether the probe weight direction $\mathbf{w}_{\text{probe}}$ causally influences conflict resolution by injecting $\alpha \cdot \mathbf{w}_{\text{probe}}$ into the last-token residual stream at a target layer during inference.
118	We measure the flip rate (fraction of samples that switch answer category) and compare against a random-direction control of equal magnitude via Fisher's exact test.
119	
120	\paragraph{L13 (mid-layer, 41\% depth).}
121	Steering at layer 13 produces significantly more behavioral change than random controls in both directions (Table~\ref{tab:steering}).
122	Positive steering ($\alpha = +5$) yields a flip rate of 19.9\% versus 6.6\% for the random control (Fisher $p = 0.002$), with all 4 directional flips moving from parametric to contextual answers.
123	Negative steering ($\alpha = -20$) yields 36.0\% versus 17.6\% (Fisher $p < 0.001$), with 5 of 6 directional flips moving from contextual to parametric.
124	Both results survive Bonferroni correction for multiple comparisons.
125	The bidirectionality confirms that the probe weight vector encodes a meaningful axis of conflict resolution: positive perturbations push toward contextual answers, and negative perturbations push toward parametric answers.
126

\section{Introduction}
\label{sec:introduction}

When multilingual large language models (LLMs) encounter conflicting information across languages, the language of presentation can determine which answer the model produces.
\citet{zhao2026when} showed that linguistic affinity dominates conflict resolution in entity-centric factual conflicts, with models preferring answers from linguistically closer sources.
Yet the internal mechanism behind this behavior remains opaque: how does the model encode the conflict signal?
Can it be detected from internal representations?
And if detectable, does the detected signal causally influence the model's resolution strategy?
These questions sit at the intersection of mechanistic interpretability and multilingual NLP, and answering them requires moving beyond behavioral observations to probe model internals directly.

Existing work on probing knowledge conflict signals has been limited to monolingual settings.
\citet{zhao2024analysing} showed that residual stream representations carry linearly detectable conflict signals in English, and \citet{boer2026probing} performed knowledge attribution probing to localize factual associations within model parameters.
Extending these approaches cross-lingually introduces additional challenges.
Translation quality may confound probe transfer: a poor translation could alter conflict detection for reasons unrelated to the conflict signal itself.
Token overlap between languages, even when minimal, could provide a shortcut for cross-lingual probes.
Observed asymmetries in transfer accuracy may reflect general cross-lingual properties rather than conflict-specific phenomena, and disentangling these sources requires careful baseline comparisons.
Beyond detectability, a fundamental limitation of probing is that it establishes correlation, not causation \citep{hewitt2019designing}.
\citet{basu2026interpretability} demonstrated that even near-perfect probe accuracy does not guarantee that the detected direction can steer model behavior.

We address these questions through a pipeline (Figure~\ref{fig:pipeline}) that combines residual stream probing with representation steering across two models of distinct architectures: Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct and Qwen3-8B.
Probes achieve 77.1\% and 75.3\% balanced accuracy on English within-language conflict detection, respectively, and all cross-lingual transfer directions exceed chance (binomial $p < 0.001$).
Cross-lingual transfer exhibits a directional asymmetry: probes trained on Chinese transfer to English approximately 7 percentage points (pp) more accurately than the reverse in both models.
This asymmetry, however, is not conflict-specific.
XNLI entailment-versus-contradiction probes \citep{conneau2018xnli} show the same directional pattern at comparable magnitude (+6.0 and +6.7 pp), with substantially overlapping confidence intervals.
The conflict asymmetry thus inherits from a general property of English-dominant models, where Chinese representations project more readily onto English representational space than the reverse.
Our causal analysis reveals a dissociation between detection and decision: the probe signal peaks at late layers (L28, 88\% depth), but representation steering succeeds only at a mid-layer (L13, 41\% depth; Fisher $p = 0.002$), with all late-layer interventions producing no significant behavioral change.
To ensure these findings are robust, we apply a confound exclusion pipeline that includes COMET-based translation quality stratification, token overlap analysis, and non-conflict baseline comparison.

These results carry two methodological implications.
The layer dissociation between probing peak and causal influence demonstrates that the layer with highest probe accuracy is not necessarily where the model resolves the conflict.
This challenges the common practice of intervening at the probing peak layer, consistent with the warning from \citet{basu2026interpretability} that detectability and causal relevance can diverge.
The directional asymmetry in cross-lingual transfer reflects a structural property of English-dominant multilingual models, not a conflict-specific phenomenon.
Any cross-lingual probing study must account for this baseline asymmetry to correctly interpret transfer differences.

Our contributions are as follows:
\begin{itemize}
    \item \textbf{Cross-lingual conflict detectability and asymmetry characterization.} We provide the first evidence that knowledge conflict signals are linearly detectable across languages in residual stream representations. The transfer asymmetry (ZH$\to$EN $>$ EN$\to$ZH by ${\sim}$7 pp) matches the XNLI non-conflict baseline in both magnitude and direction, establishing that it reflects the model's general cross-lingual structure rather than conflict-specific encoding.
    \item \textbf{Detection-decision layer dissociation.} Representation steering at the mid-layer (L13, 41\% depth) causally shifts conflict resolution (Fisher $p = 0.002$), while steering at the late-layer probing peak (L28, 88\% depth) produces no significant effect. This dissociation shows that linear detectability does not imply causal relevance, and that conflict resolution occurs upstream of where the outcome becomes linearly readable.
    \item \textbf{Confound exclusion pipeline for cross-lingual probing.} We design and validate a systematic pipeline of COMET translation quality ablation, token overlap analysis, and non-conflict task baseline comparison that excludes common confounds in cross-lingual probing studies.
\end{itemize}
